fixes.explanation: That's what he finds, friend. The Teacher saw wickedness at the very spots where you'd go looking for justice and righteousness (Ecclesiastes 3:16). Both places, not just one. I'd be shaking my head too.
I get the hope, friend. But the Teacher says he saw wickedness in both places, not fairness. It's like walking into my bakery and finding the ovens stone cold. That's not what you came for.

Not quite, friend. The Teacher says he saw wickedness in the place of judgment and in the place of righteousness. So he reports wickedness in both places, not nothing. I think that's what makes it so heavy.

Reward is a good guess, friend, but it's not the word. The Teacher ties God's judgment to a time: “…since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” I can't hand you a reward when the verse is holding out a time. Nice try, though!

That's the line, baker. The Teacher says, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” It's a hard thing to hear. In the next verse he goes on to say the fates of men and beasts are the same.

Strangers, huh? That's a plot twist, friend, but it's not in this verse. The Teacher says God tests the sons of men “…so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” The word is beasts. And the very next verse keeps going with men and animals.
Not this time, friend. The Teacher says of men and beasts, “…they all have the same breath.” So it isn't a different breath for each. He says their fates are the same, too.
That's right, baker. The Teacher says of men and beasts, “…they all have the same breath.” It isn't a different breath for each. He's building his case that their fates are the same.

Water, huh? Nice try, friend, but the Teacher says, “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” Dust is the word, both coming and going. Add water to dust and you get mud, and that's a different batch altogether.

That's not quite what he says, friend. The Teacher asks, “Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:21). It's a question, not a claim that he knows. He leaves it hanging as a question.

Right, baker. The Teacher asks, “For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” It's a question he leaves open. Right before it, he says there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work.

Leading is a different job, friend. The Teacher says, “I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter…” (Ecclesiastes 4:1). The one he names as missing is a comforter, not a leader. He says it twice in that verse.

That's the word, baker. The Teacher says, “the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” The ones holding the power are the oppressors. And once again the verse says there was no comforter.
